title: The seven beggars
hook: Rebbe Nachman's tale: beggars with apparent defects each reveal a hidden gift
tomorrow: why did the rabbi's son never reach his teacher?

segments.voice: Yesterday, hitbodedut: time each day to speak to God in your own words, on top of the words handed down. Alone with God. Today, Rebbe Nachman the storyteller.

A thrift-store mug with a chip in the rim, and somehow it's the one everybody reaches for. Rebbe Nachman told a long tale built on that kind of surprise. Two children, lost in a forest, are fed by beggars passing through: one blind, one deaf, one who stammers, one with a crooked neck, a hunchback, one with no hands, one with no feet. Years later the children marry. And at the wedding feast the beggars come back, one each day, as the wedding gift. The gift turns out to be what each one has been hiding.
screen: `A CHIPPED MUG EVERYONE REACHES FOR.` → `TWO CHILDREN, SEVEN BEGGARS.` → `THE WEDDING GIFT.`

segments.voice: Each beggar opens his flaw like a box. The blind one says: I'm not blind at all. It's that the whole time of this world isn't worth a glance to me. He's so old he remembers further back than every elder at the feast. The deaf one isn't deaf either. The world's noise is all about what's missing, and he just doesn't hear lack; to him, life is good. The one who stammers is a master of speech, so eloquent that the world's talk can't hold his words. The one with the crooked neck has a perfect voice. The flaw is where the gift lives. And each beggar blesses the young couple to be like him. Wishing a bride and groom blindness sounds like a curse, until you've heard what the blindness really was. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the tale breaks off. The seventh beggar, the one with no feet, never gets his day. Tradition says Rebbe Nachman left it untold, and Breslov Hasidim say it waits for the days of the Messiah. Once you've heard the tale, the beggars start turning up. The kid who barely talks may be the one who listens hardest. The friend who never hears the gossip isn't missing anything. The tale doesn't pretend that real suffering is secretly fine. It asks you to look twice before you decide what someone lacks.
screen: `THE BLIND ONE ISN'T BLIND.` · `HE DOESN'T HEAR LACK.` · `EACH BLESSES: BE LIKE ME.` · `THE SEVENTH DAY, UNTOLD.` · then, large: `THE HIDDEN GIFT.`

segments.voice: Pick up one object near you with a flaw: a chipped mug, a scuffed shoe, a phone with a cracked corner. Hold it for the sit and turn it slowly, letting your fingers find the flaw and stay there. Ask what the flaw shows that a perfect one couldn't: years of use, a fall survived, a story no other one has.
screen: `ONE FLAWED THING, IN YOUR HAND.` · `FIND THE FLAW.` · `WHAT DOES IT SHOW?`

howItsDone: Rebbe Nachman's tales are studied in Breslov communities and beyond, read aloud and discussed for their hidden meanings; 'The Seven Beggars' is often read slowly, one beggar's day at a time.

notes: Tale paraphrased from Sippurei Ma'asiyot 13. Details to confirm: the children are fed by each beggar in the forest and receive the blessing 'be like me'; the blind beggar's point (the time of this world is not worth a glance to him; he is the oldest, remembering further back than the elders in the ship story); the deaf beggar does not hear the world's lack; the stammerer is a master of speech; the crooked-necked beggar has a perfect voice. Hunchback and handless beggar named but not explained, for length.

'Tradition says Rebbe Nachman left it untold, and Breslov Hasidim say it waits for the days of the Messiah': Rebbe Nachman said we would not hear the seventh day until the Messiah comes; confirm framing.
Original: שבעה קבצנים from the Hebrew title 'Ma'aseh mi-Shiv'ah Kabtzanim'; the tales were told in Yiddish and printed bilingually. Confirm spelling and pronunciation.
Senses shape: an object with a flaw carries the idea; practice kind: look at (hold) one object.
